ACCEPTI find no mathematical gap in the new all-width obstruction or sparse compensation lemma, under the stated hypotheses:  $H$  remains the complete endpoint component, its displayed actual matching and six selected supports are retained, and the receiver uses the specified even-row/odd-column alignment.The accepted conclusions are
$$\rho(R_H)=1,\qquad \rho(D)\le -1,\qquad
\rho(R_H)+\rho(D)\le0$$
for every even  $w\ge4$ . At  $w=4$ , the stronger value  $\rho(D)=-2$  is forced. For every even  $w\ge6$ , the bound  $-1$  is attained by the stated feasible completion.The reservation about global donor distinctness, ownership, and coverage remains essential and is correctly stated. None of those properties is used implicitly in the local proof.1. The displayed matching and feasibility hold for every even widthThe actual matching is perfect on  $H$ :The  $w/2$  top-row edges cover all vertices  $(0,j)$ .The  $w/2-1$  lower horizontal edges cover exactly  $(1,1),\ldots,(1,w-2)$ .The two vertical edges cover the remaining lower corners and the two pendant endpoints.Consequently,
$$|M|=\frac w2+\left(\frac w2-1\right)+2=w+1,
\qquad |H|=2w+2.$$
Each of the six selected supports has exactly its designated endpoint neighbor in the baseline. There is no adjacency between selected supports. In particular, the two supports  $(3,0)$  and  $(3,w-1)$  have separation  $w-1\ge3$ , so the smallest allowed width  $w=4$  causes no exception.Every endpoint has exactly three occupied neighbors in the baseline:An interior top-row endpoint has its two horizontal neighbors and the endpoint below.A top corner has its horizontal neighbor, the endpoint below, and its axial selected support.An interior lower-row endpoint has its two horizontal neighbors and the endpoint above.A lower corner has its horizontal neighbor, the endpoint above, and its pendant endpoint.Each pendant endpoint has its matching mate and its two selected supports.Thus the configuration is feasible and single-terminal. Its only all- $P$  unit squares are the  $w-1$  squares between rows  $0$  and  $1$ . The counts and objective  $w+7$  in §1 are correct.2. The two freezing waves are acyclic and exclude mixed bundlesThe freezing proof works for actual-matching promotion bundles: a chosen matching edge contributes one promoted endpoint, its mate is deleted, and the original selected set is retained.The decisive implication is:If  $z$  cannot be promoted in a feasible bundle, then  $m(z)$  cannot be deleted by such a bundle.Indeed, deleting  $m(z)$  would require promoting  $z$ . The vertex  $m(z)$  therefore remains occupied, including when it is itself promoted. This is why the argument applies to bundles mixing colors and exterior edges.For the even-color wave, the actual mates are
$$m(z_0)=(1,0),$$
and, for  $1\le j\le w-1$ ,
$$m(z_j)=
\begin{cases}
(0,j),&j\text{ odd},\\
(1,j),&j\text{ even}.
\end{cases}$$
The last mate is
$$m(z_w)=(2,w-1).$$
These formulas verify the claimed induction throughout its full range: $z_0=(2,0)$  cannot be promoted because its two selected supports remain occupied. $z_1=(0,0)$  cannot be promoted because  $(0,-1)$  remains selected and  $m(z_0)=(1,0)$  remains occupied.At  $j=0$ ,  $z_2=(1,1)$  neighbors both  $m(z_0)=(1,0)$  and  $m(z_1)=(0,1)$ .For every subsequent  $j\le w-2$ , the coordinate formulas give the asserted horizontal and vertical incidences from  $z_{j+2}$  to  $m(z_j)$  and  $m(z_{j+1})$ .The two blocking neighbors are distinct because the earlier wave vertices are distinct and  $m$  is injective. Once  $z_j$  and  $z_{j+1}$  have been excluded from promotion, both blockers remain occupied. Promoting  $z_{j+2}$  would therefore give it at least two occupied neighbors, violating feasibility.Every dependency points to an earlier wave index. There is no circular dependence on having already frozen the other color.The wave contains exactly all  $w+1$  even-color vertices of  $H$ . Reflection
$$(r,c)\longmapsto(r,w-1-c)$$
preserves each type of displayed matching edge and permutes the six supports. Since  $w-1$  is odd, it exchanges checkerboard colors. Its reflected wave independently excludes promotion of all remaining  $w+1$  endpoints.Hence no feasible promotion bundle can use an edge of  $H$ . Exterior operations cannot defeat the certificate: they cannot delete an original selected support, and deleting an endpoint of  $H$  still requires promoting its specified actual mate.If the note is intended to stand alone, explicitly stating the promotion-bundle convention above would improve exposition. It is not a missing mathematical step in the argument under that convention.3. The positive unit is present in the original saturated-transfer ledgerIn the prescribed alignment, the relevant normalized column pairs are
$$(-1,0),\ (1,2),\ldots,(w-3,w-2),\ (w-1,w),$$
and the relevant row pairs are  $(0,1)$  and  $(2,3)$ .The physical receiver consists exactly of the following tiles:Tile typeNumber $(t,p,b)$  $s$  on deficient tilesOriginal chargeCentral full- $P$  tiles $w/2-1$  $(0,4,0)$  $0$  $0$ Upper end tiles $2$  $(1,2,1)$  $1$  each $+1/2$  eachLower tail tiles $2$  $(2,1,1)$ Saturated $0$ The four remaining receiver corners are
$$(1,-1),\quad(1,w),\quad(3,-1),\quad(3,w).$$
Each neighbors a retained selected support that already has its intended occupied endpoint neighbor. Feasibility therefore forces each corner to be blank, regardless of the exterior.This observation also resolves the potential hypothesis issue in invoking the second note. Its general tile-ownership lemma assumes global single-terminality, but no such assumption on the exterior is needed here: the explicit forced labels already show that every endpoint in  $R_H$  belongs to  $H$ . The displayed matching also keeps every mate of an  $H$ -endpoint inside  $R_H$ . The required ownership and matching closure therefore hold directly.The receiver counts are
$$|R_H|=\frac w2+3,\qquad T_R=6,\qquad P_R=2w+2,$$
giving
$$\rho(R_H)
=6+\frac{2w+2}{2}-2\left(\frac w2+3\right)
=1.$$
The table verifies this in the original ledger, without relying solely on the closed-receiver formula:Each lower tail tile is saturated and has original charge zero.Its sole endpoint is actually matched to the lower endpoint of the corresponding upper end tile.Each upper end tile therefore has  $s=1$ , raw excess zero, and original charge  $+1/2$ .Thus the positive unit is carried by the two upper end tiles. Keeping saturated tile charges at zero while deleting the deficient corrections would incorrectly remove it. The note’s warning is accurate.The baseline itself supplies a complete bundle-terminal component with positive receiver charge, so it refutes the proposed general nonpositivity rule. Its embedding is also valid: translation by  $(2,3)$  puts every occupied site within rows  $2,\ldots,5$  and columns  $2,\ldots,w+3$  of the stated  $8\times(w+8)$  grid. Both dimensions are even, and
$$w+7<\frac{8(w+8)}2=4w+32.$$
There is no conflict with the global coefficient-one target.4. The donor has at most one occupied vertex in arbitrary feasible complete-component exteriorsWrite
$$a=(2,1),\qquad b=(2,2),\qquad
c=(3,1),\qquad d=(3,2).$$
The physical tile  $D=\{a,b,c,d\}$  is aligned and lies outside  $R_H$  for every allowed width, including  $w=4$ .The occupancy proof correctly separates feasibility from component completeness: $a$  is blank. It has the two distinct endpoint neighbors  $(2,0)$  and  $(1,1)$ , so it cannot be selected. It cannot be an endpoint because it would then join the complete endpoint component  $H$ . $c$  is blank. The selected support  $(3,0)$  already has the occupied neighbor  $(2,0)$ . Any occupancy at  $c=(3,1)$  would give that support a second occupied neighbor. $b$  cannot be an endpoint. It neighbors  $(1,2)\in H$ , so endpoint occupancy would contradict completeness of  $H$ .If  $b$  is selected, then  $d$  is blank. The selected vertex  $b$  already has its occupied neighbor  $(1,2)$ . If  $b$  is blank instead, only  $d$  remains available for occupancy in  $D$ .Therefore
$$t+p\le1.$$
This proof makes no assumption that the donor is a no- $P$  tile. In particular,  $d$  may be an endpoint of another component.Since  $t\le1$ ,  $D$  is deficient. Its actual saturated-transfer count satisfies
$$0\le s\le p.$$
Using the original charge formula from the dependency gives
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho(D)
&=t+\frac p2-2+\frac s2\\
&\le t+p-2\\
&\le-1.
\end{aligned}$$
This remains valid when  $p=1$  and  $s=1$ ; the potentially incoming half-unit is fully retained. Together with the already established receiver charge, it proves
$$\rho(R_H)+\rho(D)\le0.$$
There is no hidden raw-charge substitution or no- $P$  assumption in this deduction.5. The width-four strengthening, sharpness, and endpoint example are correctWidth fourFor  $w=4$ , the right pendant endpoint is  $(2,3)$ . Consequently  $b=(2,2)$  has two endpoint neighbors,  $(1,2)$  and  $(2,3)$ , excluding selection; completeness excludes endpoint occupancy.Also,  $d=(3,2)$  neighbors the selected support  $(3,3)$ , which already neighbors  $(2,3)$ . Hence  $d$  is blank.All four donor sites are therefore blank, and
$$\rho(D)=-2,\qquad \rho(R_H)+\rho(D)=-1.$$
Sharpness for every even  $w\ge6$ In the blank baseline, all four neighbors of  $(3,2)$  are blank. The left lower support is at column  $0$ , at distance two; the right lower support is at column  $w-1\ge5$ , at distance at least three. None of the other supports is adjacent either.Adding  $(3,2)$  as a selected vertex is consequently feasible. It preserves  $H$ , its matching, its completeness, and all receiver labels. It gives
$$(t,p,s)=(1,0,0),\qquad \rho(D)=-1.$$
Thus  $-1$  is genuinely attained for every even  $w\ge6$ , and the combined local budget can be exactly zero.An endpoint can occupy the donorThe example adding
$$(3,2)\!-\!(4,2)$$
is also feasible for every even  $w\ge6$ . Neither endpoint is adjacent to  $H$  or to a displayed selected support, so this is a separate endpoint component. The edge fits inside the specified embedding.The mate  $(4,2)$  lies in the tile with normalized rows  $4,5$  and columns  $1,2$ . That tile has no selected vertices and is deficient. Hence, in  $D$ ,
$$(t,p,s)=(0,1,0),\qquad \rho(D)=-\frac32.$$
The added component is not single-terminal. The note explicitly allows this and uses the example only to establish that an arbitrary feasible exterior before normalization need not leave  $D$  in the no- $P$  complement. That use is sound.6. The aggregation warning is necessary and correctly preserves the remaining gapFor pairwise disjoint physical regions
$$C_i=R_{H_i}\cup\{D_i\},$$
the original tile ledger gives
$$\rho(\mathrm{grid})
=
\sum_i\bigl(\rho(R_{H_i})+\rho(D_i)\bigr)
+
\sum_{Q\notin\bigcup_i C_i}\rho(Q).$$
Applying the local inequalities once yields
$$\rho(\mathrm{grid})
\le
\sum_{Q\notin\bigcup_i C_i}\rho(Q).$$
That is the valid aggregate consequence. A global bound still requires control of the remaining charge.In particular, if  $D_i$  lies in another component’s receiver, one cannot use both its charge as a payment for  $H_i$  and that other receiver’s unchanged whole-region budget. The tile would be counted twice. Removing it from the latter receiver instead requires a new bound for the remaining region; the old closed-receiver identity cannot simply be reused for the punctured region.The first note correctly leaves open:Distinctness of the assigned donor tiles.Exclusion of donors from other receivers whose full budgets are already being used.Coverage of every positive receiver.Any replacement argument using larger disjoint receivers with fully established budgets.Those are genuine remaining global obligations. The new local lemma neither proves them nor silently assumes them.No required repair emerges from this written review. The reported census, control programs, and Lean receipts play no role in the acceptance above; all requested conclusions follow from the all-width coordinate arguments and the original physical tile ledger.
